title: I Gave Google AI Studio a Product Idea.

It Built the Damn Thing. Day 5 of 30 Days of Code. Dhananjay Trivedi 24 min read · Just now -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Open Sourced Project and the App link is attached at the bottom of this story. I have been running my startup (bhama.app) for over two years now and I have to get a lot of NDAs signed by many Interns / Team Members who have been working on the sensetive data on our app and system. Getting a tailored document, keeping track of it, etc takes a lot of switching between chats and document management. And this app should be free for us. So, The basic thought was simple: someone creates a document, shares it with another person, that person reviews it, understands the important clauses, accepts it, and the owner gets an activity trail. But my thoughts weren’t exactly organized. Feature here. Problems there “Maybe we should do this.” “What if we also…” “And then perhaps…” You know how product conversations go when you’re still inside your own head. Then I added one line to my prompt that changed the entire interaction: And yeah, like I might be missing something as a product owner or as an expert product manager or whatever helps, help me restructure my thoughts and redefine the idea so that we can just give that to our Google AI Studio. I wasn’t asking it to code. I was asking it to think with me. And that’s when things got interesting. I stopped trying to be the smartest person in the room The AI took my messy product thinking and turned it into an actual product brief. It came back with: Build a Legal Document Review & Acceptance Web App — V0 Mock UI And suddenly the idea had shape. It defined two users. An admin who creates and shares documents. And a viewer who receives the link, reviews the document, understands the important terms and accepts it. The core flow became: CREATE ↓ SHARE ↓ OPEN ↓ UNDERSTAND ↓ AGREE ↓ PROVE That was the product. Not twenty-seven features. Not a massive roadmap. Just one loop. And this was the first thing I realized: AI becomes much more useful when you stop treating it like a code generator and start treating it like a product-thinking partner. Then I did something that would’ve normally taken me hours I asked it to define the entire V0. Not production infrastructure. Not authentication. Not Firebase. Not real email. Not real electronic signatures. Just the product experience. The specification became surprisingly detailed. PIN gate. Admin dashboard. Create document. Document preview. Document detail. Share modal. Document viewer. AI-generated key terms. Signer details. Acceptance confirmation. Activity timeline. Responsive behaviour. Mock data. Service abstractions. Even the future architecture. And I deliberately told it what not to build. Do NOT implement Firebase yet. Do NOT implement real authentication. Do NOT implement real notifications. Do NOT connect to external AI APIs. Do NOT implement real electronic-signature infrastructure. That mattered. Because I’ve learned this lesson the expensive way: The fastest way to make an AI agent slow is to give it permission to build everything. A good MVP isn’t just a list of features. It’s a list of things you’re refusing to build. The interesting part was the viewer The most important screen wasn’t the dashboard. It was the document itself. I wanted the recipient to read the entire legal document in one continuous view. No fake pages. No unnecessary pagination. Just the document. Then I wanted AI-generated key terms sitting beside it. Something like: [ Confidentiality ] [ Non-disclosure ] [ 2-year obligation ] [ Intellectual property ] [ Termination ] [ Governing law ] But these weren’t search buttons. They were navigation. Click “Confidentiality” and the app should take you to the actual confidentiality clause and highlight it. That distinction was important to me. The AI can summarize. But the original document remains the source of truth. So the interface also included: AI-generated summary. Review the original document before accepting. AI should help someone understand a document. It shouldn’t pretend to replace the document. Then I asked the obvious question The prompt was getting huge. At this point I had basically handed Google AI Studio a miniature product specification. And I thought: Can Google AI Studio actually handle this? I gave it the work. It started implementing. I looked at the clock. Two minutes had passed for me. Then five minutes of implementation. Seven minutes total. I actually had to laugh. Because normally, this is where I’d start thinking about the team. Product owner. Designer. Two developers. QA. Tickets. Git branches. Standups.
